en: Taal Volcano features a crater lake on Volcano Island, which sits inside the much larger Taal Lake, creating an island within a lake within a volcano.
Found in Bohol, the Philippine tarsier has eyes as large as its brain and can rotate its head a full 180 degrees to spot prey.
Mount Apo in Mindanao is the highest peak in the Philippines, standing at 2,954 meters, and serves as the primary habitat for the critically endangered Philippine eagle.
Laguna de Bay has no natural water outlet, so its water level is strictly controlled by the Manggahan Floodway to prevent flooding in surrounding provinces.
The Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park in the Sulu Sea is a UNESCO World Heritage site accessible only by liveaboard boats for three months each year.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park features a navigable underground river that flows through a massive cave before emptying directly into the West Philippine Sea.
Baguio City receives an average of over 300 centimeters of rain annually, making it one of the wettest and coolest cities in the entire Philippines.
The island province of Camiguin has more volcanoes, with seven, than it has municipalities, which only number five.
The Philippines holds the second-largest gold reserves in the world, alongside massive copper and nickel deposits, making it one of the most mineral-rich countries globally.
Maria Cristina Falls in Iligan City generates about half of the hydroelectric power for the entire Mindanao region, earning the area the nickname City of Waterfalls.
The Chocolate Hills in Bohol consist of over 1,200 perfectly cone-shaped limestone mounds that turn brown during the dry season, resembling giant chocolate kisses.
The Philippine Sea contains the Philippine Trench, which plunges over 10,500 meters deep, making it one of the deepest oceanic trenches on Earth.
